# The Irreversibility Ledger {#sec-ledger}

Part II has arrived at a place where the useful questions have stopped being numerical. The
existence grid says which numerical reasoning is available; the convexity chapter says the sign of
your response to dispersion. Neither produces a decision.

This chapter supplies the instrument that does, and it is deliberately primitive. It is a two-sided
account.

**On one side: exposures you can exit at an acceptable cost. On the other: exposures that can
produce an absorbing state — a position from which there is no continuing.**

The rule for using it is one sentence: **the irreversible side is closed to new entries until it is
empty or bounded.**

## Why an account rather than a criterion

The idea of avoiding ruin is not new, and stating it as a criterion invites the obvious objection
that everyone already tries to avoid ruin. The difficulty is not knowing the principle. It is
noticing, in a live situation with a hundred competing considerations, which of the exposures on the
table belong on the second side.

An account forces that noticing, in the same way that a balance sheet forces a firm to notice what
it owes. The instrument is boring on purpose. **Boring instruments get used; elegant criteria get
admired.**

## What makes an exposure irreversible

Four mechanisms, and they are worth separating because the remedies differ.

**Physical.** The state cannot be restored by spending money. Only prevention helps. A species lost, an aquifer drained, a
patient's organ damaged. The remedy is prevention, because there is no repair.

**Contractual.** Exit is possible, but only with the agreement of someone who has no reason to grant it. Terms are the remedy. A long-dated supply commitment, a lease, a loan covenant. The remedy is terms: shorter
duration, staged commitments, break clauses.

**Informational.** The exposure reveals something that cannot be un-revealed. Smallness is the remedy. A strategy becomes
visible when scaled; a position announces itself through its own market impact. The remedy is
deliberate smallness.

**Social.** Exit costs reputation or standing, and the cost is borne by a person rather than an institution. Procedures are the remedy. Admitting an error publicly, abandoning a project one championed. The remedy is
structural: pre-commit to a review, so that exit is a procedure rather than a confession.

The fourth mechanism is the one most often missing from risk registers, and it is the one that
explains why organisations persist with losing positions long after the arithmetic is clear. **The
cost is real and it falls on individuals, so it belongs in the account.**

## The exit-cost question

For each entry, three questions, and the answers should be written down.

**What is the worst-case cost of exit?** Not the current cost. The cost in the state of the world
where you most need to exit, which is usually the state where everyone else needs to exit too.

**How long does exit take?** A position that can be closed in an hour is not the same exposure as
one that takes a year, even if the accounting value is identical.

**Whose agreement is required?** Exits requiring a counterparty, a regulator, a board, or a
co-investor are slower and more expensive than exits requiring only a decision.

The systematic error here is **present-state bias**: exit costs are estimated under current
conditions, when the relevant costs are those under stress. Every entry in the account should carry
a stress-case exit cost, and where that estimate is unavailable, the entry should be treated as
worse than it appears.

## The bounding move

Five ways to convert an irreversible exposure into a bounded one. They are the practical content of
the chapter.

| Move | What it does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cap the size | Limits the maximum loss to a chosen number | Position limits, capped commitments |
| Shorten the term | Reduces the window in which conditions can turn | Staged contracts, rolling agreements |
| Add a second source | Removes single-point dependence | Dual suppliers, portable skills |
| Buy the option rather than writing it | Makes the loss bounded and known | Insurance, break clauses, reversible pilots |
| Pre-commit the exit | Converts a judgement into a procedure | Review dates, stop rules set in advance |

The last move is the cheapest and the least used. A stop rule agreed before the position exists
costs nothing and removes the social cost of exit, because the decision was made by a previous
self. **Its value is that it addresses the fourth mechanism directly, and the fourth mechanism is
the one that keeps people in losing positions.**

## A worked entry

Take the supply case from Chapter 8 and write it as an account entry.

**Exposure.** Dependence on a single counterparty for a critical input.

**Mechanism.** Contractual, with a secondary social component, since the relationship was championed
internally by a specific manager.

**Stress-case exit cost.** Prepayment at risk, plus a search period during which production slows.
Under stress, alternative suppliers are themselves constrained, so the search period is longer than
the current estimate suggests.

**Stress-case exit time.** Between six and twelve months.

**Whose agreement.** The counterparty's, for release; the manager's, for the reputation component.

**Bounding move chosen.** A second qualified supplier developed in parallel, with a pre-committed
review at twelve months.

Note what the account did. It did not estimate a probability of counterparty failure. It did not
produce an expected loss. **It identified an exposure whose stress-case exit is slow and whose exit
requires the agreement of someone with a reputational interest in not exiting, and it prescribed a
structural change.**

## Refutation conditions

Three ways this instrument could fail.

**Exit costs are systematically underestimated, including stress-case ones.** If the account is
populated with optimistic exit costs, the second side will be under-populated and the instrument
will provide false comfort. The mitigation is procedural: require a stress-case figure and treat
its absence as a red flag rather than a gap.

**The instrument may collapse into a list.** A ledger that records everything classifies nothing,
and an entry-level account of a complex organisation can become an inventory. The defence is the
closure rule: the account is used to decide what to do next, not to document what exists.

**The closure rule may be too rigid.** "Closed to new entries until empty or bounded" could block
projects whose irreversible components are small relative to their value. The rule is meant to force
the bounding conversation, not to prohibit action, and a reader who applies it as a prohibition has
misread it.

## The ledger applied to itself

**What transformation should it survive?** Changes of domain: it should work for a firm, a
household, and a public body.

**Does it?** The four mechanisms and the bounding moves are domain-general, and they require no
quantities. What does not travel cleanly is the standard for "acceptable cost", which depends on
resources and on appetite. The account's output is a structure, not a threshold.

**Verdict.** A grade II construction, like the others in this book.

## Claim and tool

The claim: irreversible exposures require separate accounting, because they are not comparable to
reversible ones and because they are systematically missed in ordinary risk review.

The tool: the two-sided account, the four mechanisms, the stress-case exit questions, and the five
bounding moves.

Registered as B-007, with the refutation conditions above attached. It is the instrument Part IV
uses to order decisions, and it is the second half of the book's central metaphor: **the Constant
tells you what survives; the Ledger tells you what you cannot afford to lose while finding out.**

## Boundary conditions

The account presumes that exposures and their exit costs can be identified, which is itself a
judgement and often contested inside organisations.

It presumes that someone is willing to write entries that name individuals' social costs, which
requires a culture that tolerates being explicit about them.

And it does not weigh the two sides against each other. The closure rule is a rule, not a
calculation, and it is meant to be followed before the comparison is made rather than after.

## Populating a ledger without it becoming a form

The ledger's value depends entirely on the quality of its entries, and the quality depends on how the
exercise is run.

**Do it in a group.** Written first, discussed second. The reason is the fourth
mechanism: the social exposures are precisely the ones that individuals are reluctant to name in front
of the sponsor of the project. Written entries collected before discussion produce different and better
lists than a facilitated conversation.

**Require a stress-case exit cost.** Its absence is a finding. An entry without one is
either a misunderstanding or a hope, and saying so in the room is the instrument's main contribution
to a project that is going well.

**Separate exposure from response.** Two passes. The exercise goes wrong when each exposure is immediately
paired with a mitigation, because the pairing converts the accounting into a negotiation. The first
pass lists exposures and mechanisms; the second pass, run separately, generates the bounding moves.

**Name the date before the meeting ends.** Always. A pre-committed exit is only pre-committed if it is
recorded somewhere before the position exists, and the recording is the whole of the mechanism.

**What good looks like.** One page. A one-page list with four columns, entries that name individuals' social
costs without embarrassment, at least one exposure that the sponsor did not know about, and a review
date. **If every entry is marked bounded, the exercise has failed and the failure is visible on the
page.**

## The ledger and the fourth quadrant

The two devices are separated in this book by several chapters and they belong together, so the
connection is worth stating explicitly.

The fourth quadrant describes a class of problems: fat-tailed outcomes with payoffs that depend on
magnitude. The ledger is an instrument for one property of those problems, the existence of an
absorbing state.

**What the ledger adds.** The action, not the map. The quadrant map tells you that the standard apparatus does not apply. It
does not tell you what to do. The ledger supplies the action: enumerate the irreversible exposures,
bound the ones that can be bounded, and remove the ones that cannot.

**What the quadrant adds.** Shape, not size. A ledger with no notion of distribution shape will treat a
bounded exposure under a thin-tailed process and a bounded exposure under a fat-tailed one as
equivalent, and they are not: the second has a meaningfully higher chance of the bound being reached.
**Bounding limits the loss; the shape of the tail determines how often the limit is approached.**

**Why the order is ledger first, then quadrant.** Because the ledger's question is structural and
answerable without data, while the quadrant assignment requires judgements about tail behaviour that
are contested. **Front-loading the structural question means the decision is already safer before any
contested judgement is made.**

## Ledger entries for a household

The ledger is presented in this book with institutional examples. Its most direct use is smaller, and
the smaller version is a better introduction to the instrument.

**A house. Physical and financial.** Irreversible in the sense that selling takes months and the price
is not chosen. Mechanism: contractual and physical combined. **Stress-case exit cost: the price in the
state of the world where the household must sell, which is usually the state where the local labour
market has weakened.** Bounding move: the equity buffer, which is the only one available.

**A specialised career. Informational and social.** Irreversible in the informational sense: the skill
becomes visible and its applicability narrows. **Stress-case exit cost: the time to rebuild
transferable capability, not the salary foregone.** Bounding move: portable credentials, documented
work, and a network that does not depend on one employer.

**A health decision with a permanent component. Physical.** No bounding move available on the harm side,
so the screen is applied to the timing: is there a reversible trial, a second opinion with a stopping
rule, a waiting period that changes nothing.

**A public commitment. Social.** The cost falls on the person rather than the institution, and the
remedy is structural: **pre-commit the review, so that the exit is a procedure rather than a
confession.**

**What the four share.** Each is a case where the decision is usually made on the merits and the
irreversibility is not discussed. **Writing the third column takes ten minutes per entry, and the third
column is where the surprise is.**

## The ledger as a negotiating instrument

The ledger is described as an analytical device for the decision-maker. It is also an instrument for
negotiation, and the second use is often the more consequential.

**What the ledger gives a negotiator.** A named list of exposures with mechanisms, exit costs and required
agreements. **Three of those four fields are facts about the other side of the transaction, and facts of
that kind are leverage.**

**Three specific applications.**

**Exit costs and counterparty behaviour.** A stress-case exit cost that requires the counterparty's
agreement is a cost the counterparty controls. **Naming it converts an implicit dependency into a term to be
negotiated, which is how break clauses get written.**

**The social mechanism.** An exposure whose exit cost is reputational for a specific person is not
negotiable with the institution, and identifying it changes who the conversation is with. **This is the most
practical use of the fourth mechanism and the one least often described.**

**The residual category.** Exposures that cannot be enumerated must be bounded by structure, and caps are
negotiable. **A request for a cap is easier to secure than a request for a forecast, and it addresses the
same risk.**

**What the ledger does not do in a negotiation.** It does not establish that the deal is bad. It converts
unstated dependencies into stated ones, which changes the terms rather than the decision. **The distinction
matters because a party who presents the ledger as an objection will lose the benefits of presenting it as a
specification.**

**Why this belongs in the chapter.** Because the instrument's adoption in practice depends on someone
carrying it into a room where the terms are set, and a tool presented only as a private discipline will stay
private.

## The ledger for a committee

The ledger works for an individual and changes character in a group, and the changes are worth anticipating.

**Three dynamics in a committee.**

**Exposures are under-named.** Each member can see exposures that touch their own remit and is reluctant to
name exposures that implicate someone else's. **The result is a complete-looking list that omits the social
and informational exposures, which is exactly the category the instrument exists to surface.**

**Bounding moves are proposed too early.** A committee's instinct is to solve. **The pairing of exposure with
remedy converts the accounting into a negotiation, and the list is never finished.**

**The residual category is treated as an admission of ignorance.** Members prefer a list that looks complete.
**The honest answer — that some exposures cannot be enumerated — reads as incompetence in a group setting.**

**Three procedural responses.**

**Collect written entries before the discussion.** Each member submits exposures separately.

**Separate the two passes.** Exposures and mechanisms first; bounding moves in a later session.

**Require the residual category explicitly.** A named cell for exposures that cannot be enumerated, with a
structural bound attached. **Making it a required field converts an admission into a deliverable.**

**What the committee version produces.** A longer list than the individual version and a more honest one.
**The instrument's value in a group is not the analysis; it is the fact that the fourth mechanism becomes
sayable.**

## The ledger after a failure

The instrument is presented for decisions. Its most instructive use is after an irreversible failure, when the
question is what the account would have shown.

**What the retrospective exercise reveals. Three things.**

**Which exposures were named and which were invisible.** The entries a firm would have written before the failure
are usually fewer and milder than the situation warranted. **The gap is the instrument's diagnostic value, and it
is specific: the missing entries cluster in one of the four mechanisms.**

**Which bounding moves were available.** Almost always at least one, and usually one that would have bounded the
loss without abandoning the activity. **The availability of a bounding move is the difference between a failure
and a catastrophe.**

**Which review dates would have intervened.** A pre-committed review scheduled before the failure would have
forced the question at a moment when the answer could still change. **The absence of a review is the most common
finding, and it is the cheapest to fix.**

**How to run the exercise. Three steps.**

**Reconstruct the account as it was.** From documents and decisions made at the time, not from memory after the
fact.

**Mark the entries that were missing.** Name them and their mechanisms.

**Ask what the review would have asked.** Not what the firm should have known, but what a scheduled review would
have surfaced.

**What the exercise is not.** An attribution exercise. **Its purpose is to improve future lists, and an exercise
that identifies a person's failure produces defensiveness and no improvement. An exercise that identifies a
missing mechanism produces a longer list next time.**

**Why this section matters for adoption.** Because an instrument that has never been used retrospectively is
believed on the strength of its argument. **An instrument that has been applied to a known failure has a track
record, and a short one is better than none.**

## The ledger and the option to wait

Waiting is a decision, and the ledger has a specific contribution to make to it: the recognition that delay is
itself an exposure.

**Three ways delay creates exposure.**

**Option value decays.** An opportunity not taken is often gone, and the ledger's own logic applies to it.
**Waiting is irreversible in one direction, which is the direction of not having acted.**

**The world moves.** Conditions favorable to the decision can change while the review proceeds. **A delayed
decision is made under different conditions from the ones it was deferred for.**

**The social mechanism operates during the delay.** The longer a project waits, the more its sponsors are
invested in it, and the harder the eventual refusal becomes. **Delay is not neutral with respect to the fourth
mechanism.**

**What the ledger says about waiting. One rule.** Treat the delay as an entry. **Name what is being given up,
estimate the cost of the delay in the same three fields as any other exposure, and record the date by which
waiting stops being free.**

**What the rule prevents. Two failures.**

**Waiting as an unexamined default.** Which is the common case: a decision deferred because deferring is
costless in the short run.

**Waiting justified by a quantity that will not improve.** The deferral fallacy of the second interlude, and
the ledger supplies the addition that the delay itself has a cost.

**What the rule does not do.** Decide. **It converts waiting from a non-decision into a decision with a cost,
and the conversion is what the ledger is for.**

**Why this entry is often missing from the list.** Because delay is not usually described as an exposure, and
the ledger's four mechanisms are read as applying to commitments rather than to withholdings. **A list that
includes only the commitments will systematically favour waiting, which is a bias the instrument can correct
once it is pointed out.**

## The ledger and the smallest decision

The instrument is presented for decisions with stakes. Its cheapest and most frequent use is on decisions that
look too small to warrant it.

**The case. A small commitment.** A contract renewal, a hire, a tool adoption, a supplier change. **Each is
individually unremarkable and the four mechanisms apply to all of them.**

**What the ninety seconds produce. Two questions.**

**Is any part of this irreversible.** A renewal at a higher price, a hire with notice periods, a tool with data
lock-in, a supplier with a qualification cycle. **The answer is usually yes in a smaller way than the earlier
examples and the same in kind.**

**What is the exit cost under stress.** Which is where the small decisions differ from the large ones: the
stress-case cost is usually bounded, and the exercise's value is confirming that rather than assuming it.

**Why the small decisions matter in aggregate.** Because they are numerous. **A firm's exposure profile is
determined by its ordinary commitments more than by its exceptional ones, and the ordinary ones are the ones
nobody lists.**

**Three signs a small decision needs the ledger.**

**The exit requires someone else's agreement.** A notice period, a counterparty's release, a regulator's
approval. **The first field of the instrument.**

**The knowledge involved lives in one person.** The informational mechanism.

**The commitment was championed internally.** The social mechanism. **Which is the most common and the least
noticed in small decisions, because the champion is usually a colleague rather than an executive.**

**What the ledger does not require for small decisions.** A page. **Two questions and an answer, recorded in
whatever document the decision already uses. The instrument's value in this range is that it converts a habit
into a check, and the check is what stops the aggregate exposure from accumulating unexamined.**

**Why the section is short.** Because the application is short. **A method whose cheapest case takes ninety
seconds is one that can be applied to ordinary decisions, and the ordinary decisions are where the exposures
come from.**

## The ledger and the four mechanisms in one table

The four mechanisms are presented with examples. Their remedies, costs and monitoring differ, and a table of the
differences is what a practitioner needs.

**Physical. Remedy: prevention.** Cost: the activity foregone. Monitoring: the state of the physical system.
**The only mechanism with no bounding move on the harm side, which is why prevention is the whole remedy and why
the exposure is bounded before the activity rather than during it.**

**Contractual. Remedy: terms.** Cost: the price of the flexibility, paid in the negotiation. Monitoring: the
clause and the counterparty's standing. **The mechanism most amenable to bounding, because terms are written
before the commitment.**

**Informational. Remedy: size.** Cost: the return foregone by staying small. Monitoring: public data, which is
where the exposure would appear. **The mechanism whose remedy is a scale rather than a structure.**

**Social. Remedy: procedure.** Cost: the effort of a pre-committed review. Monitoring: whether the review
happened. **The mechanism that is invisible in risk registers and that explains persistence in losing
positions.**

**What the table shows. One asymmetry.** Three of the four have remedies that are chosen before the commitment;
the physical one does not. **Which is why the physical mechanism's exposures must be bounded by not taking them,
and why the other three can be managed after the decision to proceed.**

**How to use the table. One pass per exposure.** Name the mechanism, then read the remedy and the monitoring off
the row. **Which takes a minute and replaces the general question "what could go wrong" with a specific one.**

**What the table cannot supply. The exit cost.** Which requires the three questions of the instrument's earlier
section and is the field most often missing. **The table gives the remedy and the monitoring; the exit cost is
computed per exposure.**

**Why the table is worth having.** Because the four mechanisms are otherwise read as a list of examples, and the
list gives no guidance. **Four rows, one remedy each, and the social row is the one that practitioners do not
already have.**

## The ledger and three comparisons it makes unnecessary

The instrument's value is often stated as a benefit. Three specific analyses it makes unnecessary are worth
naming, because each is expensive and each is avoided.

**Estimating the probability of the absorbing event.** Which is usually impossible and which the ledger's rule
avoids by requiring the exposure to be bounded regardless. **The rule does not need the probability, which is why
it applies where the probability cannot be estimated.**

**Valuing the irreversible exposure in present-value terms.** Which requires a discount rate over an indefinite
horizon. **The ledger replaces the valuation with two questions about mechanism and exit cost, and neither
requires a rate.**

**Optimising the portfolio of exposures against a utility function.** Which requires preferences over states the
organisation may never see. **The ledger's rule is a constraint rather than an objective, and a constraint can be
applied without a utility function.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is an analysis the standard framework requires and the
ledger avoids. **Which is the instrument's efficiency claim: it substitutes structure for estimation where
estimation is unavailable.**

**What the ledger gives up by avoiding them. Two things.** The ranking of exposures by severity, and any
comparison with risks that are reversible. **Both are real losses and neither is available in the cases the
ledger addresses.**

**How to state the trade. One sentence.** The ledger trades a ranking for a constraint. **Which is the right trade
where the exposures are unbounded and the wrong one where they are not, which is why the instrument's first
question is whether the exposure is irreversible at all.**

**Why the three are worth naming.** Because the ledger is presented as a discipline and its practical appeal is
that it avoids expensive analyses. **Three unnecessary analyses, one constraint, and the avoidance is the reason
the instrument is usable in the settings where the others are not.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The instrument is proposed by this book. There is a substantial literature on real options and on
irreversibility in investment, which the chapter does not survey, and I make no claim that the four
mechanisms are exhaustive.

The example is constructed from the Chapter 8 case rather than drawn from a documented episode, and
the stress-case exit estimates in it are illustrative.
